title: Marimba
reference_instrument: Iowa MIS marimba (model NA; bar material not stated; yarn, cord and rubber mallets)
summary: A struck rosewood bar, not yet a marimba: A3, Gb2 and the scale's eight notes, C4 to C5, have a resonator tube and only Eb6 has none, the hard rubber mallet isn't the recording's, and the undercut is solved in the engine and not measured. Those ten notes now take the bar's loss from one printed whole-bar loss factor, eta 0.0045 from H. Hill's unrefereed 2011 student report, tried after seeing that the notes decayed too fast on a law fit through three printed rosewood bars, and f1 now decays far closer to the recordings: on A3 its two lines each fall at 48 dB/s (70 and 71 on the earlier law) against the recording's 31.4, on C5 the line that stays at 77.2 (129.7) against 59.7, and on Gb2 f1 now lasts longer than the recording's, 12.1 dB/s against 21.9. On every note the tube makes the line that stays fall faster than the bar's own law. Eb6 is still on the earlier law. The outline comes from J. La Favre's table of an unnamed commercial 5-octave marimba, and the stiffness and density from the rosewood row of Chaigne and Doutaut 1997. Iowa states no bar wood or outline, so this isn't the recording's bar. A3 is a bright knock, its 2017 Hz mode within 40 dB of f1 for about 180 ms while f1 swells for 171 ms. Eb6 is close to one decaying sine, set against a recording that is a roll. On Gb2 f1 is the strongest line, 6.5 dB over the bar's third bending mode; the recording's f1 leads its third mode by 31 dB.
physics_present: The bar outline from J. La Favre's table of an unnamed commercial 5-octave marimba with rosewood bars, on a 56 x 6 x 3 mesh, and G4 on 56 x 6 x 4, A4 on 56 x 8 x 5, B4 on 56 x 8 x 6 and C5 on 56 x 8 x 4, each with its cut solved again there, because origin's boundary-element floor refuses the coarser mesh at their bands
Rosewood stiffness and density from Chaigne and Doutaut 1997 (JASA 101, Table I): E 2.13e10, density 1015. The other elastic ratios are Honduras mahogany's, a stand-in (USDA Wood Handbook)

The bar's loss on A3, Gb2 and C4 to C5: one printed whole-bar loss factor, eta 0.0045 at every mode, 1/tau = pi eta f, the mean as printed, with the printed range 0.0036 to 0.0068 as its limit. It is from H. Hill's unrefereed 2011 student report (NSF REU, University of Illinois Physics 406): the bars of a Yamaha YM-5100A, Honduras rosewood per the maker's spec for that model, recorded in a room with the resonators off, so eta holds the wood, the cord and the bar's own radiation, and the tube adds only its own losses. The stiffness and density stay Chaigne and Doutaut's, so the loss and the stiffness come from different rosewoods. It was tried after seeing that the notes decay too fast on the earlier law, and no recording number entered it. Hill measured the six C bars, C2 to C7, so every f1 here lies inside that span. Eb6 is still on the earlier law, fit through three printed rosewood bars, gamma_B 14.526 1/s and eta 1.0759e-6 s: Bremaud and Sprossmann, both Dalbergia latifolia, and Brancheriau, an unidentified Dalbergia; it spans 393 to 945 Hz, so every Eb6 mode is extrapolated on it

A circular-arc undercut solved in the engine from the modes alone, for f1 at equal temperament and f2 = 4 f1, the tuning the builder states for its own padouk bars; the third mode isn't aimed at. On Eb6 the arch length is the one the builder prints on its padouk table and only f1 is solved, because the builder says that register is tuned to the fundamental only. On Gb2 the arc runs to the blank's length limit and only its middle is solved, for f1 alone, leaving 5.498 mm of 23.37 mm; f2/f1 comes out 3.991, untargeted
A Hertz contact mallet, Chaigne and Doutaut's hard rubber row at 1.0 m/s, with the strike point carried from the xylophone bar
Burton-Miller boundary-element radiation up to the band each page states, with no box

On A3, Gb2 and the scale's eight notes, C4 to C5, a closed tube under the bar, coupled both ways: La Favre's tube for that note from his own padouk marimba, not this bar's instrument, with its stop set to this bar and each bar mode exchanging with its nearest tube mode alone. On Hill's loss the tube's first mode loses more than the bar on every one of them, and on Gb2 and C4 to C5 by more than the coupling can bridge, so f1 is one frequency with two decays; on A3 the two lines still split, by 0.28 Hz, and start nearly opposite in phase, so f1's band has no dip before it is 130 dB under its peak. On B4 the stop's one solve leaves the tube's first resonance 0.06 Hz above f1, the others within 0.03 Hz. La Favre prints no air column for Gb2's tube, only its total length, and his is mitered in 3 sections where ours is straight
physics_missing: A resonator tube on Eb6: a real marimba hangs a tuned tube under each bar, and here every note but Eb6 has one. At equal modal velocity A3's f1 radiates 32 dB less than its third mode. The A3 recording has lines at 3.00, 5.00 and 7.00 f1 and we don't know what they are: they fall at 50-52 dB/s where this tube's odd modes lose 334, 911 and 1952 dB/s by the printed laws, and on our clip the tube's lines sit 42 to 53 dB under them

The recording's mallet: the Gb2, A3 and C5 recordings use a cord mallet, and Eb6's is a roll with no mallet named. The recordings differ in mallet as well as tube, and these renders can't separate the two

The right decay: on Hill's loss f1 decays far closer to the recordings, but not onto them. On A3 its two lines each fall at 48 dB/s (70 and 71 on the earlier law) against the recording's band at 31.4; read the recording's way, from 100 ms past the band's peak, f1 falls 38.0 (64.2 on the earlier law), slower than either line because the lines come into phase across that read; on C5 the line that stays falls at 77.2 (129.7 on the earlier law) against 59.7; on Gb2 the f1 band falls 12.1 dB/s against the recording's 21.9 (22.9 on the earlier law), its two lines at 14.2 and 20.2, so f1 now lasts longer than the recording's. On the scale's eight notes the line that stays falls at 52 to 77 dB/s. On every note the tube makes it fall faster than the bar's own law, which gives 11.4 dB/s on Gb2, 27.0 on A3 and 32 to 64 on C4 to C5. Chaigne and Doutaut write that marimba bars have lower internal damping and stronger tube coupling than xylophone bars, and that decay times with and without the tube clearly differ on marimbas in the low range. Nothing was aimed at the recordings: the stops sit on each bar's f1, the tube's loss is the printed laws' and the bar's is one printed number. Eb6's recording is a roll, so it gives no decay to compare
A printed undercut: the rosewood table prints no arch length and no tuning, so we don't know that a maker would cut what the engine solved
The recording's bar: Iowa states no bar wood and no bar outline
Any mode above the band each page states: nothing above it is in that file

A receiver that holds during contact: each page's peak but Gb2's, which comes just after contact, and those that are now the tube's bloom, C5's at 49.2 ms and A4's and B4's in the scale, is a pulse from the contact force through the receiver law, not the note's level, as tested on F4 with a second receiver. The engine's broadband modal observer landed in fbf0863b1 as an optional receiver: on F4 it passes that second-receiver test during contact, but on A3, C5 and Eb6 it didn't grade closer, so the pages keep the narrow-band receiver, and it refuses cards with a tube
